title: Pelican AI turns big banks’ costly false alarms into a profitable business
excerpt: Disseminated on Behalf of: Pelican AI Corp. All figures in Canadian dollars unless otherwise noted. Already profitable, Pelican AI is targeting roughly 65% revenue growth and continued positive adjusted EBITDA for 2027 as it scales its marketing and sales reach. Customer-reported results include a 96. 8% straight-through processing rate at a global American bank and a reduction of more than 70% in false positives at a Big 5 Canadian bank. Its new Fraud Alerts Optimizer, launched Sept. 17, 2026, gives banks a way to filter out false fraud alarms, and Pelican is now adding bank pilot partners. Banks are being squeezed from two directions. Payment volumes keep rising, and each payment must clear a widening set of regulatory checks before it reaches its destination. The industry is increasingly turning to artificial intelligence to manage that load, using it to automate payment processing, anti-money laundering (AML) checks, sanctions screening, and fraud detection to lower operating costs. Grand View Research projects the global AI in banking market will reach US$143. 56 billion by 2030, growing at roughly 31. 8% a year. Pelican AI Corp. (CSE: PEL) has been building this kind of software for 33 years, well before the trend had a name. The Toronto-based company works across three core areas of a bank: a payments platform that moves money faster with fewer manual fixes, a compliance suite covering AML, sanctions screening, and fraud detection, and trade finance tools that scan global shipping deals for signs of money laundering. Its clients include Wells Fargo, BMO, TD, Intesa Sanpaolo, Standard Chartered, and State Bank of India, spread across more than 55 countries, and the company began trading on the Canadian Securities Exchange on Sept. 1, 2026. “Banks spend money on AI, regulatory compliance, and process automation,” said CEO Nino Di Teodoro. “We live at the intersection of all three of those. ”. AI before it was called AI. Plenty of fintechs now describe themselves as AI companies. Pelican has been doing the work for 30 years, back when the industry still called it machine learning. Over this time, it has processed more than two billion transactions for the largest global banks. That history matters because a large bank can always outspend a small software vendor on technology, but it cannot buy decades of real-world transaction data. “They can buy the latest and greatest,” Di Teodoro said. “What they don’t have is the decades and literally billions of transactions that we’ve seen. That makes our models sharper and more accurate than anything they can produce. ”. The hidden cost of a false alarm. To understand why banks pay for Pelican’s software, it helps to look at how a payment actually moves. Payments are a high-volume, low-margin business, and the industry measures itself by straight-through processing, the share of transactions that travel end to end without anyone touching them. When a person has to step in, the bank usually ends up losing money on that payment. False positives are the biggest cause of those interventions. A legitimate payment can stall over something as small as a missing space in a surname, or an address on a street that happens to share a name with a sanctioned individual. Large banks employ hundreds, sometimes thousands, of people to clear these exceptions every day, and most still fall behind. “I don’t know of any bank that actually looks at every single alert that they get,” said Di Teodoro, who previously ran fraud and financial crimes at Symcor, the payments processor jointly owned by RBC, TD, and BMO. Pelican’s software learns from those human reviewers. It watches how operators resolve each false alarm, then applies the same fix automatically the next time a similar case appears. Clients say the difference shows up in their numbers. A global American bank using Pelican reports a 96. 8% straight-through processing rate and says it handled 28% more volume without adding staff, saving $2. 3 mil

title: Bank of America warns against giving AI agents a banking password
excerpt: Bank of America warns against giving AI agents a banking password. By OpenTools Team · October 28, 2026. A customer email warns against sharing login credentials with AI agents. The bank’s existing guidance separates passwords from supported data access and explains revocation limits. The warning concerns passwords given to an outside agent. Bank of America is warning customers against giving their banking username and password to an AI‑enabled service that offers to act for them. A customer email posted publicly on October 27 explicitly includes AI tools and agents in its warning about sharing credentials. TechCrunch reported that a bank spokesperson confirmed the email’s authenticity. The message says customers are responsible for activity resulting from access they provide by sharing credentials. That is the bank’s stated warning. It does not establish the outcome of a disputed transaction, change every customer’s legal rights or document an actual loss caused by an AI agent. The immediate question for someone connecting a financial assistant is what access the service is requesting. Handing over the password is different from granting a supported service a defined connection to account data. Supported data sharing uses a different access mechanism. Bank of America’s official third‑party data‑sharing guidance describes a consent‑based mechanism in which the customer signs in directly with the bank rather than giving a third party their login credentials. The bank says this reduces the information a connected service can access and removes the need for that service to store and use the customer’s password. The guidance contrasts this with credential sharing: a service holding the login may have the same access to account information as the customer, without a choice about how much information it retrieves. The bank also warns that access can continue after a person stops actively using the service. These distinctions concern access to account information. The FAQ does not certify a particular AI assistant, establish that every service uses the supported connection, or grant an agent permission to make payments. A product describing itself as an assistant does not, by that description alone, identify how it connects to a bank. Revoking access does not erase previously shared information. For services using its supported protocol, Bank of America says customers can view connected third parties and revoke permission in Mobile or Online Banking. Its guidance treats services using shared login details differently, describing a password change as the most secure way to stop that form of access. The bank separately warns that a third party may retain information it has already received. Removing an ongoing connection and deleting previously collected data are therefore different questions; the FAQ points readers to the third party’s own privacy and retention policies for the latter. The AI‑specific email is a current warning, while the reviewed data‑sharing FAQ has no established publication date. It should not be presented as a newly introduced October 27 policy. Together, the sources explain why password sharing and supported consent‑based access deserve separate treatment, without establishing a bank breach or the safety of any particular agent. title: Understanding the banking industry's reaction to AI agents
excerpt: Artificial Intelligence. BankThink. Understanding the banking industry's reaction to AI agents. By Greg Baer and Paige Pidano Paridon. Published October 28, 2026, 7:30 a. m. EDT. 5 Min Read. Facebook. Twitter. LinkedIn. Email. Key insight: The introduction of AI agents capable of transacting on behalf of their customers has many banks placing restrictions on their use. But the reason for banks' caution is not well understood, and is sometimes misrepresented. Forward look: it seems likely that if customers want to use AI agents to act on their behalf, the security and legal liability issues will be resolved through private negotiations, industry standard setting, regulatory actions, legislation or litigation. And eventually there could be an effect on deposit betas. But we are a long way from there. The potential effect of agentic AI on banking has become a topic across media and this quarter's bank earnings calls. Much commentary, however, misunderstands what is at stake and what is motivating banks to take some of their recent actions. Agentic AI in banking includes two major use cases. One involves an agent accessing a customer's account to make payments or otherwise transact. A second involves an agent managing the customer's account — either maximizing yield by regularly sweeping funds from a deposit account to a higher-yielding product or reducing the customer's risk by moving uninsured deposits out of a struggling bank. These use cases raise four important questions that should not be conflated. Question 1: Will customer use of AI agents increase cyber and fraud risks? As we have seen online fraud explode in volume, defensive work has focused on confirming customer identity; increasingly, that verification will be biometric. Agentic AI, however, can obfuscate identity and bypass a bank's fraud controls designed to verify that there is a human in the loop, and that the transaction is not the product of a rogue or hallucinating agent. Banks are still developing tools to manage this risk. Question 2: Who is responsible in the event an agent makes a mistake — for example, sends money to the wrong place or orders the wrong item? Certainly, Muse's terms of service disclaim practically all legal liability to the user, and anyone hoping to contact Meta or Muse will likely find no one available to help with the problem. Unhappy customers will inevitably call the bank that processed the payment. Thus, for banks (and one hopes, policymakers) to be comfortable with agentic transactions, liability and responsibility will have to be established through private sector negotiations, regulatory actions, legislation or litigation. Question 3: Will the use of agents to move deposits to higher-yielding products increase banks' deposit betas — how much they pay for deposits in comparison to market rates? Of course, depositors wishing to maintain deposit insurance protection already have an incentive to increase the yield they earn on their cash by moving excess cash to savings accounts or CDs. For those seeking even higher yields, the concept of sweeping excess cash to a money market fund is ages old, and corporate customers negotiate fee waivers and other allowances in exchange for holding deposits. title: Agentic AI can cut banks' transaction monitoring workload by up to 50%: McKinsey
excerpt: Synopsis. Banks could reduce the human effort required for transaction monitoring investigations by 30-50% by deploying agentic artificial intelligence (AI), while improving the quality and consistency of compliance reports, according to a report by McKinsey. Listen to this article in summarized format. Banks could reduce the human effort required for transaction monitoring investigations by 30-50% by deploying agentic artificial intelligence (AI), while improving the quality and consistency of compliance reports, according to a report by McKinsey. The report said AI agents could handle data collection, research, analysis and report preparation, allowing human experts to focus on complex cases, risk assessment and final decisions. "In transaction monitoring investigations, we have seen banks achieve a more than 40 percent reduction in human processing time," McKinsey said, adding that reports generated by AI agents showed higher completeness against predefined checklists than analyst-written reports. Unlike tools that assist individual analysts with specific tasks, agentic AI can coordinate an entire investigation, from gathering information across systems to preparing documented recommendations. McKinsey said this could help banks respond to increasingly sophisticated financial crime threats while managing the growing time and resources required for compliance. The report said AI-generated reports could also improve consistency by using the same transaction analysis periods and report structures across cases, with claims linked to their source data for review by quality teams, auditors and regulators. However, McKinsey stressed that human oversight remains essential. AI agents can analyse evidence and make recommendations, but people must assess findings, address gaps in information and retain responsibility for decisions. "AI augments our work, but all judgments remain with our team," Hans-Georg Beyer, Commerzbank's chief credit risk officer and former group chief compliance officer, said in the report. McKinsey said banks seeking to scale the technology should build systems with quality checks, clear risk controls and traceable decisions. It noted that 30-50% of an agent network may need to be dedicated to quality assurance and traceability. The report also said the same approach could be extended beyond transaction monitoring to fraud detection, know-your-customer checks and regulatory compliance. One large bank used a multi-agent system based on similar principles to prepare corporate credit risk assessments, halving the time credit officers spent on analysis. McKinsey said banks should begin with a focused use case, demonstrate its value and then expand to wider compliance activities. It cautioned that successful adoption would depend not only on technology and data access but also on staff skills, continued collaboration between compliance experts and data scientists, and robust governance. The report said banks would need to monitor deployed AI systems closely, test their reliability and make continuous improvements as risks and business requirements evolve. title: Powens launches Connector Agentic Factory, an AI system to build and fix Open Finance connectors
excerpt: Powens launches Connector Agentic Factory, an AI system to build and fix Open Finance connectors. Press Release | News 28 Oct 2026. Source: Powens. Powens, a leading European Open Finance infrastructure provider, today announced the launch of its Connector Agentic Factory, an internal AI system that is capable of building new Open Finance connectors and repairing existing ones. Connectors are the technical links that let banks, fintechs, and financial apps securely retrieve a customer’s financial data, or make payments, from a bank or other institution. Powens maintains more than 1,800 of them across Europe, and they underpin the services that banks, fintechs, lenders, wealth platforms, and software vendors offer their own customers. Until now, repairing a broken connector could take up to two days of engineering work, and building a new one up to three weeks. The Powens Connector Agentic Factory changes that. To build a new connector, the system examines how a given institution’s systems work and creates the connection accordingly within a couple of hours. 12 new connectors have already been delivered this way across Europe, spanning banking, wealth, and document data sources. To repair an existing connector, it investigates what went wrong and proposes a fix, cutting a typical repair from up to two days down to 10–15 minutes, with 50% of its proposed fixes directly approved by Powens engineers, a rate that keeps improving as the system matures. The result is faster expansion of coverage, faster recovery when something breaks, and a higher quality of service for the customers who rely on Powens. The technology operates with human oversight at every stage: every proposed connector or fix is checked and approved by Powens engineers before it goes live, ensuring the reliability and accountability the financial industry demands. AI does not manipulate data or payments; it is exclusively used to build and maintain connectors that remain deterministic and secure in nature. Jean Guillaume, chief executive officer of Powens. “Our ambition is to unlock the full potential of Open Finance and build the best infrastructure in Europe, covering every type of data and delivering unparalleled levels of quality and coverage in every market we serve,” said Jean Guillaume, chief executive officer of Powens. “Powens’ Connector Agentic Factory is a direct expression of that ambition: AI lets us raise the bar on reliability and extend our coverage across Europe faster, without ever compromising on control. ”. “Powens’ Connector Agentic Factory represents a shift in how we think about Open Finance infrastructure,” added Fabien Oliveira, chief product & tech officer at Powens. “It means our engineers spend less time on repetitive diagnostic work and more time on higher addedvalue activities such as improving the factory or the user and agent experience, which is exactly where we want their expertise focused. ”. The announcement comes days after Powens’ Connector Agentic Factory was named Best Use of AI in Open Finance at the Open Banking Expo Awards on October 13th in London. Powens’ Connector Agentic Factory can already be used to repair any Powens connector, while its connector-building capability currently focuses on investment and savings, with plans to extend to additional connector types in the coming months. For Powens, it’s also a proof point: an early, concrete example of how AI can be applied safely within regulated financial infrastructure, an approach the company expects to extend to other parts of its platform over time. By Anand Pandya. Institutional banking meets its next counterparty. For decades, institutional banking has operated around a simple assumption: there’s a human on the other side of the relationship. A portfolio manager calls the desk. An analyst logs into a research portal. A trader asks for pricing. The workflows, controls, compliance frameworks, and relationship models across the industry were all built around that idea. That assumption is starting to change. Increasingly, the first interaction may not come from a person at all. It may come from software acting on the client’s behalf. Institutional banking is entering an agent-to-agent era, in which software acting for the client deals with the bank’s systems and, increasingly, with the bank’s own AI. AI systems on the buy side are beginning to retrieve research, query pricing, access analytics, and in some cases initiate execution through programmatic interfaces. The human hasn’t disappeared from the relationship. But the access layer is becoming automated. That isn’t a subtle shift. In certain parts of the market, client-side AI agents are already interacting directly with bank infrastructures. That work matters, but it’s not the biggest structural shift underway. The more important development is that institutional clients themselves are adopting AI quickly, especially hedge funds, quantitative firms, and large asset managers that already operate through highly automated infrastructure. Prime brokerage is the clearest example. Clients already consume position data, financing data, margin analytics, and risk information through APIs and structured interfaces. Moving from traditional APIs to AI-agent-driven access is not a massive leap technically. The gap is rarely “how do we do it” but “do we know how we did it”. What’s missing is the governance layer. Canada's largest bank will block third-party personal artificial intelligence agents from direct access to its digital properties, such as online banking. Toronto-Dominion Bank said it will block all third-party personal AI agents from direct access to banking information where authentication is required. "Our focus is on helping build a future where trusted AI agents can create meaningful value for clients while protecting their privacy, security and control over their financial information," a spokesperson said. Bank of Nova Scotia said it will limit third-party AI agents from accessing banking platforms, while National Bank of Canada said it is monitoring the development of consumer AI agents, such as Muse, and assessing both the opportunities they may create for clients and the associated risks. Bank of Montreal said it does not permit AI agents to access its digital properties or execute transactions. An AI agent is a piece of software that does things autonomously for its users. "That is a risk front and centre for us. AI has sort of moved along the capabilities curve. ". OSFI is also considering whether the financial system requires an AI safety code, though Routledge did not provide details on what such a code would look like. "Maybe it plays a useful role in elevating basic standards to a minimum level, so we have some semblance of confidence that across the financial system there's a basic level of safety and protection," he said.
